name: Daily Streak
classificationRationale: A streak counter is a game-inspired structure — a running score that resets on failure — rather than a plain reminder, so it is classified as a Gamification Mechanic.
definition: A visible count of consecutive days (or sessions) in which a user has completed a qualifying action, which resets to zero if a day is missed.
operation: Each day the user completes the qualifying action (e.g. one lesson), a counter increments; the product displays the current count prominently, often with an icon, and the count returns to zero after a missed day unless a safety-net variant is in play.
variants: Purchasable or earnable 'freeze' / insurance item that preserves the streak across one missed day
Decoupling the streak requirement from a larger daily goal, so any minimal qualifying action (not a full session) extends it

psychologyLinks.qualification: Loss aversion is commonly offered as the explanation for why streaks motivate — the fear of losing an existing count outweighs the appeal of extending it — but this is an interpretive frame, not something verified for every implementation.

risks: Can produce guilt- or anxiety-driven engagement rather than intrinsic motivation, a frequently raised critique of streak mechanics generally
An all-or-nothing reset can discourage return after a single lapse unless a forgiving variant is offered

name: Shared Streak
classificationRationale: This extends the streak game structure to two or more participants with mutual stakes, so it remains a Gamification Mechanic rather than a purely social feature.
definition: A streak counter maintained jointly by two or more users, which continues only while every participant keeps completing the qualifying action.
operation: A user invites one or more others; the streak becomes active once the invitation is mutually accepted. Each participant must independently complete the qualifying action for the shared count to continue, and participants can typically prompt each other to act before the day ends.
variants: Reminder or 'nudge' prompts sent to a lagging participant by the others sharing the streak

psychologyLinks.qualification: Framed as mutual commitment / social accountability — people are more reluctant to let a shared obligation lapse than a private one — though the scale of the effect will vary by relationship and product.

risks: May favour users who already have an engaged social circle, limiting it as a growth lever for isolated or new users
Reported associations between shared streaks and completion are easily confounded by self-selection — already-engaged users are more likely to set them up in the first place

name: Progress Ring / Completion Meter
classificationRationale: A fillable, 'closeable' visual meter is a game-inspired progress structure (directly analogous to a quest or XP bar), so it is classified as a Gamification Mechanic.
definition: One or more visual meters that fill as a user accumulates progress toward a personal goal within a fixed period (typically a day), and are explicitly marked 'complete' once the goal is reached.
operation: The product tracks one or more underlying metrics continuously, maps accumulated value onto a ring, bar or similar shape, and visually signals closure (e.g. the ring joins up) once the goal threshold is met. Multiple independent rings can track different dimensions of the same broader behaviour at once.
variants: Personalised, periodically-adjusted goal thresholds rather than one fixed target for all users
Adapted metrics for different user populations (e.g. crediting wheelchair pushes rather than steps)

psychologyLinks.qualification: Visible, incremental progress toward a near goal is widely used to sustain effort; the specific magnitude of effect for any one ring design has not been independently verified here.

risks: A daily reset can make a single missed day feel like a complete loss rather than a partial setback, similar to streak mechanics
No independently published outcome study was located for this pattern as implemented in the seed example — the description here covers mechanics, not proven effectiveness

name: Adaptive Daily Goal
classificationRationale: A tunable target with a defined success threshold is a goal/challenge game structure, classified as a Gamification Mechanic.
definition: A daily target whose size can be set or adjusted — by the user or the product — independently of other mechanics (such as a streak) that depend on reaching it.
operation: A user is assigned or chooses a goal size (e.g. lesson intensity). The product may separately decide how much of that goal is actually required to satisfy a connected mechanic, and can adjust the required threshold based on observed behaviour across its user base.
variants: Lowering the bar for a connected mechanic (e.g. a streak) independently of the stated goal size, to prioritise consistency over volume

psychologyLinks.qualification: Letting users choose goal intensity speaks to autonomy; separately, lowering the bar for a connected mechanic is a product design choice about trade-offs, not a claim about any single psychological mechanism.

risks: Reducing the bar required to satisfy a connected mechanic can decouple the signal of 'success' from the amount of underlying activity actually performed

name: Achievement Badges / Awards
classificationRationale: A collectible marker awarded for reaching a milestone is one of the brief's own listed examples of a game-inspired structure, so it is classified as a Gamification Mechanic.
definition: A discrete, collectible signal — a badge, award or trophy — granted when a user reaches a defined milestone, personal best, or participates in a time-limited event.
operation: The product monitors for qualifying conditions (a personal best, a milestone count, participation in a seasonal event) and grants a visual award to a persistent collection the user can review.
variants: Seasonal or time-limited awards tied to a calendar event rather than an open-ended milestone

psychologyLinks.qualification: Badges mark discrete progress points and can reinforce a sense of accumulating achievement; whether that translates into sustained behaviour change beyond the collecting itself is not established here.

risks: Can shift attention toward collecting badges as an end in itself rather than the underlying behaviour the badge was meant to recognise

name: Informal Social Competition
classificationRationale: A scored, time-boxed comparison between participants is a competitive game structure, classified as a Gamification Mechanic.
definition: A lightweight, often opt-in contest in which participants' activity is scored and compared over a fixed, short period.
operation: Users opt in and share relevant activity data with each other; the product scores each participant (e.g. by percentage of a goal met) over a fixed window and surfaces the comparison, typically alongside ordinary progress tracking rather than replacing it.
variants: Ongoing passive sharing of progress with friends/family without a formal time-boxed contest

psychologyLinks.qualification: Social comparison can be motivating for some users and discouraging for others; the product's choice to make this opt-in is one way of managing that variability, not evidence that it works uniformly.

risks: Sharing personal activity or health data, even opt-in, can create social pressure some users find uncomfortable

name: Personalised Year-in-Review
classificationRationale: This turns a user's own historical data into a personalised narrative with no points, levels, streaks or competitive structure — a behavioural engagement technique rather than a game structure — so it is classified as an Adjacent Engagement Pattern.
definition: A periodic, personalised summary of a user's own activity data, presented as a shareable narrative or story rather than as a functional report.
operation: The product aggregates a defined window of a user's historical activity data, applies ranking/weighting rules to surface standout items, blends algorithmic selection with editorial design, and packages the result as a shareable, visually distinct artifact separate from the product's everyday interface.
variants: Separate editions tailored to different audiences (e.g. end listeners versus creators/artists) from the same underlying data

psychologyLinks.qualification: Personalising and narratively framing a user's own data increases its salience and shareability; this describes a plausible attention mechanism, not a measured causal effect specific to any one edition of the feature.

risks: Converts otherwise-private behavioural data into a public artifact, which raises data-sensitivity considerations even when sharing is optional
Methodology choices (time windows, exclusions, weighting) shape the output in ways most users are not positioned to evaluate

name: Personalised Nudge / Reminder
classificationRationale: A targeted reminder or prompt is a general behavioural-engagement technique with no inherent game structure of its own — it is classified as an Adjacent Engagement Pattern, though it is frequently paired with mechanics such as streaks.
definition: A message prompting a user to complete a qualifying action before a deadline (commonly the end of the day), personalised to the user's own status or sent by another participant on their behalf.
operation: The product (or another user, in a shared-mechanic context) detects that a qualifying action has not yet been completed within a relevant window and sends a prompt, often timed close to the deadline and referencing the user's specific status (e.g. an at-risk streak).
variants: Peer-sent 'nudges' from another participant in a shared mechanic, rather than a system-generated message

psychologyLinks.qualification: Timely, personalised prompts near a deadline are a standard behavioural-reinforcement technique; effectiveness depends heavily on frequency and relevance, which varies by product and was not independently measured here.

risks: Poorly tuned frequency or tone can shift from helpful reminder to perceived nagging, risking notification fatigue or opt-out

name: Activity History Heatmap
classificationRationale: This visualises historical activity with colour-coded feedback but defines no objective, streak rule, score or competitive rank — a behavioural feedback display rather than a game structure, so it is classified as an Adjacent Engagement Pattern, not a streak.
definition: A calendar-style grid showing a rolling period of a user's historical activity, where colour intensity per cell represents the relative volume of qualifying actions that day.
operation: The product tracks qualifying actions against rule-based eligibility criteria, aggregates them per day, and maps the daily total onto a colour scale from low to high intensity across a fixed rolling window (e.g. the past year).
variants: Showing anonymised activity counts from otherwise-private context without exposing the underlying details
Accompanying numeric totals (e.g. a running count) alongside the visual grid

psychologyLinks.qualification: A persistent visual history can make recent gaps and accumulated activity salient; this is a plausible feedback mechanism, not evidence the grid was designed or shown to increase activity frequency.

risks: Can reward raw frequency more visibly than the quality or impact of the underlying activity
Users may read blank cells as a negative signal even when inactivity was appropriate or intentional
Rule-based eligibility criteria can make the display diverge from a user's own intuitive sense of their activity

name: Social Signalling / Public Profile
classificationRationale: Making activity visible to others is a reputational/self-presentation mechanism, not a game structure with an objective, score or competitive outcome, so it is classified as an Adjacent Engagement Pattern.
definition: Displaying a summary of a user's activity or history on a profile that other users can view, independent of any explicit ranking or reward.
operation: The product surfaces an activity summary (e.g. a history grid, badge collection or stats panel) on a profile page visible to other users by default or by choice, without itself scoring or ranking that activity against others.
variants: Default public visibility with an opt-out
Visibility limited to connected users (e.g. followers) rather than everyone

psychologyLinks.qualification: Public visibility may create reputational or self-presentation incentives; documented here as a plausible mechanism from the product's own visibility design, not a measured behavioural effect.

risks: Can encourage performative activity aimed at how a profile looks to others rather than the underlying work itself
Visibility defaults matter — public-by-default shifts incentives differently than opt-in visibility

name: Leaderboard
classificationRationale: An ongoing ranked comparison of participants' results against a shared, repeatable benchmark is a competitive game structure, classified as a Gamification Mechanic — distinct from a short, time-boxed informal contest.
definition: A persistent ranked list of participants' results against a shared, repeatable benchmark (such as a fixed course or task), rather than a one-off or time-boxed contest.
operation: The product matches qualifying results to the shared benchmark, ranks eligible participants by a chosen metric, and lets a participant filter the ranking (e.g. by time period or demographic group) or restrict the view to just their own results.
variants: Filtering the leaderboard to demographic or equipment categories (e.g. age or weight group)
Restricting a participant's own results to a private, non-ranked view of just their own history on the same benchmark

psychologyLinks.qualification: Public rankings introduce comparison and competition; effects plausibly vary by a participant's ability and whether they find ranking motivating or discouraging — not established as uniformly motivating in the reviewed sources.

risks: Can demotivate lower-performing or less competitive participants
Where the benchmark is physical or geographic, results can be affected by conditions or equipment rather than effort alone
May encourage unsafe or excessive effort in pursuit of rank

name: Personal Best / Record
classificationRationale: Tracking and visibly marking a user's own best result over repeated attempts is a game-score structure (a personal high score), classified as a Gamification Mechanic.
definition: A tracked record of a user's own best result on a repeatable benchmark, visually marked and plotted against their historical attempts.
operation: The product records each qualifying attempt at the same benchmark, identifies the best result by the relevant metric, marks it distinctly among the user's plotted history, and updates it whenever a new best is achieved.
variants: Letting the user set a target result for a specific benchmark to work toward

psychologyLinks.qualification: Concrete feedback against a stable, repeatable task plausibly supports mastery-oriented goal pursuit; the reviewed sources describe the feature, not a measured effect on adherence or performance.

risks: Stable benchmarks can still be affected by external conditions, so a 'best' result may not purely reflect improved effort or skill

name: Time-Limited Challenge
classificationRationale: A finite, deadline-bound target with a defined reward or completion state is a goal/challenge game structure, classified as a Gamification Mechanic.
definition: A challenge that defines one or more qualifying actions, or a measurable target, to be completed within a fixed window, after which it expires whether or not it was met.
operation: The product defines qualifying actions or a target metric and a start/end time, tracks progress against that target during the window, and marks the challenge complete — often with a reward — if the target is met before the deadline; the challenge otherwise lapses unmet.
variants: Personalised or account-specific challenge terms rather than one challenge offered identically to all users
A distance, count or spend-based target rather than a single qualifying action

psychologyLinks.qualification: A concrete target with a visible deadline is a standard goal-gradient / urgency device; this describes the design, not measured evidence that it changes behaviour beyond what would have happened anyway.

risks: A hard deadline can create pressure to act sooner, more often or more intensely than a user would otherwise choose
Personalised or account-specific terms can make challenges difficult for users to compare or fully understand

name: Reward Currency
classificationRationale: A persistent, accumulable in-product currency earned through qualifying actions and redeemable for value is a core game-economy structure, classified as a Gamification Mechanic.
definition: A virtual currency or points balance that accumulates as a user completes qualifying actions, and can later be redeemed according to the product's current rules.
operation: The product credits a user's currency balance on completing qualifying actions — including, in some cases, bonus amounts from time-limited promotions — maintains the balance as part of the broader account, and allows redemption against a published or evolving set of options.
variants: Bonus or promotional currency awarded for completing a specific time-limited challenge, in addition to the standard earn rate

psychologyLinks.qualification: A currency credited for qualifying actions is a contingent-reward structure; the reviewed sources describe the mechanic, not an isolated measurement of its effect on purchasing or usage behaviour.

risks: Can incentivise actions taken mainly to earn currency rather than for their own value
Redemption rules and currency value can change over time, affecting the real worth of an accumulated balance

name: Named Progress Levels
classificationRationale: Naming discrete tiers that a user advances through based on completed steps is a levelling game structure, classified as a Gamification Mechanic.
definition: A small set of named tiers representing increasing completion or mastery, which a user advances through by completing specific recommended steps, with the current tier and next step shown prominently.
operation: The product defines an ordered set of named tiers, each requiring a specific number or set of completed steps; it evaluates the user's current completed steps against each tier's threshold, displays the current tier and the next incomplete step, and removes or changes the display once the top tier is reached.
variants: Keeping the tier status private to the user rather than displaying it to other users
Removing the level indicator entirely once the top tier is reached, rather than leaving a permanent marker

psychologyLinks.qualification: Naming discrete tiers and showing the next concrete step is consistent with goal-gradient effects, but the reviewed sources document the design, not a measured effect on completion rates.

risks: Can encourage standardised completion of recommended steps even where a step isn't relevant to a particular user
A top-tier label can imply quality or value when it may only reflect field completion

name: Community Challenge
classificationRationale: Aggregating multiple participants' individual contributions toward one shared, measurable target is a collective-goal game structure, classified as a Gamification Mechanic.
definition: A challenge in which the qualifying activity of many participants is summed toward one shared target, rather than each participant having their own separate goal.
operation: The product defines a shared target and a window, aggregates each participating user's qualifying activity into a running collective total, and displays the combined progress toward the shared target to participants.
variants: Allowing a user to create a custom version of the challenge and invite specific other participants, rather than only joining an open, product-run one

psychologyLinks.qualification: A visible collective target can introduce cooperative or accountability dynamics; the reviewed sources describe the design, not a measured effect on individual participation.

risks: An individual's contribution can feel insignificant against a large collective total, particularly at scale
Aggregated totals can mask very uneven contribution levels among participants
